extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, trial lawyers, judges, forensic psychologists, and investigators evaluating witness reliability
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing the reliability, credibility, and informational quality of witness testimony by analyzing perception, memory, language, education, temperament, time estimates, and situational factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition for valid comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons by a witness are reliable only if the items compared are parallel, close together, and start from the same level; if things cannot be juxtaposed they lead to bad comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the witness discovered the 'right juxtaposition' before relying on comparative testimony; poor or forced juxtapositions indicate the comparison is likely invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest-driven selectivity of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception and interpretation depend on what interests the witness: people perceive and remember primarily what matters to them (e.g., a child remembers only the chocolate, not the whole man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the witness had motive or personal interest that would focus attention on particular details; if so, expect omissions or distortions of surrounding facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic variability and word-connotation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Words function as symbols and can connote different things to different people; the same word may evoke different complex concepts for different listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when witnesses use abstract or ambiguous terms; explore what they personally mean by a contested word and avoid assuming dictionary equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of foreign expressions and mistranslation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using foreign words or expressions in evidence is dangerous because their sense often does not coincide with dictionary meanings or our usage (e.g., 'love' vs 'amour').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid foreign terms when precise meaning matters; if used, require explanation of the witness's intended sense to prevent misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulating small semantic mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Small differences in word-meaning and associations multiply and can make a witness's version of events substantially different from reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe for associative meanings and connotations attached to key terms; consider semantic drift over time or across social groups when reconciling testimonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-interval time perception inaccuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Most people have no idea of the duration of very small times (minutes/seconds); they will markedly underestimate short intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on unanchored short-interval estimates; where exact minutes matter, corroborate with clocks or other time-keeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting short-time estimates with external aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Two means of correction: have the witness determine time in terms of a familiar reference (e.g., a paternoster) or give the witness a watch to observe the second hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, elicit time estimates anchored to familiar cyclic events or demonstrably observed clock readings rather than free estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-period estimates require event anchors
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates of longer periods (weeks, months, years) are only credible when fixed by distinct events; without such anchors they are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask witnesses to tie dates to verifiable events (harvests, holidays, other incidents); treat unsupported chronological claims with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating hasty earlier estimates as fixed reference points
rubrics_metrics.description: A hasty statement (e.g., 'it happened four years ago') can become a fixed point around which later reasoning is structured, producing cascading errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test and revisit early, rough temporal assertions rather than allowing them to anchor subsequent inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider both nature and nurture in character/credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's nature (innate disposition) and nurture (education, environment, experience) together determine what a person is and how they will behave; both must be considered when judging testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate background, upbringing, and inherent traits together; don't assume education alone predicts truthfulness or resilience to wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of education as predictor of honesty or criminality
rubrics_metrics.description: Education does not straightforwardly reduce criminal behaviour; statistical and empirical evidence do not show that increased literacy necessarily decreases all crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic inferences that literate or educated witnesses are more truthful; examine conduct and context case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as a possible but unreliable reliability indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'really religious person' may be assumed more reliable, but religious/statistical data are often worthless or indeterminate for assessing criminality or credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming religious sincerity as evidence of reliability, require concrete proof of genuine belief; do not rely on denomination statistics (e.g., 'Protestant' vs 'Catholic') which are meaningless without measuring true faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uneducated witnesses: assimilation vs reproduction deficit
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncultured/uneducated persons often cannot assimilate perception in its integrity and reproduce it simply; they confuse perception with inference and tend to see only the nearest characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect simplification, conflation of inference and observation, and incomplete accounts from uneducated witnesses; corroborate and probe systematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid multi-part and complex questions with uneducated witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneducated people tend to answer only the last part of a compound question; complex, multi-clause questions produce unreliable answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pose single, simple, clear questions; break compound inquiries into separate, plain questions to obtain usable testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of uneducated witnesses to verify by touch
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneducated persons often feel new objects rather than merely look at them, using touch to confirm identity when sight is deemed insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that tactile verification may indicate limited trained observation; when possible, consider this behavior when judging their visual identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic identification unreliability among the uneducated
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneducated people may misread photographs, attend to backgrounds, and mistake contours, so denials or confirmations of photographic identity have little value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat photographic ID from uneducated witnesses with skepticism; investigate the witness's perceptual and representational habits before accepting photographic identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of picture-derived misconceptions (size, proportions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas learned from pictures (e.g., relative animal sizes) can persist despite later correction and bias memory and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discrepancies arise, explore whether prior pictorial representations could have implanted mistaken beliefs that shape the witness's testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-sided education and overgeneralization risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons with specialized or one-sided education may appear generally educated but actually lack knowledge in other fields and thus may overreach or mislead outside their specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a witness has narrow expertise, force disclosure of limits via careful questioning; do not let expertise in one field unduly elevate credibility on unrelated matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autodidacts and dilettantes tend to overestimate competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-taught persons commonly measure the value of their knowledge by their own effort and therefore often overestimate and assert beyond their competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check claims by autodidacts; press for concrete evidence of training/experience rather than relying on asserted effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts' incidental pride (hobby expertise) can mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts sometimes take pride in incidental, less-relevant accomplishments (hobbies) and this can induce undue respect that causes their unrelated assertions to be taken at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to halo effects from incidental skills; evaluate each claim on its own merits and relevant expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclination vs opportunity/need distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclination (a person's tendency) must be distinguished from opportunity, need, or desire; capacity and repeated successful acts can interact with inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate calling, lifestyle, spouse choice, leisure preferences, and other long-term indicators to infer inclination rather than assuming behavior stems solely from opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statistics and detailed life-history to assess inclination
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical patterns and thousands of small biographical details are necessary to differentiate types (e.g., true tramp vs unemployed person) and infer genuine inclinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on aggregated behavioral patterns and careful biographical inquiry rather than single observations to infer propensity or inclination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament labels are of limited practical use
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient four-humor temperament categories (choleric, sanguine, phlegmatic, melancholy) are imprecise and changeable; temperament alone does not reliably determine character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer describing observable traits (cautious, reflective, active) and test them empirically rather than relying on fixed temperament categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as diagnostic of observer's character
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject, manner, and timing of a person's laughter can indicate their level of education and outlook; what a person laughs at reveals the nature of the observer as much as the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe affective reactions such as laughter to gain supplementary insight into a witness's perspectives and cultural position; use as one data point among many.
